narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped just above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score of 23 was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Compared with the average of 37 among accepted students, this score signaled that you would likely struggle with the exam.

Next, your family income bracket of lower-middle had a meaningful but opposite effect, pulling the prediction somewhat toward passing. While this helped your case, it was not enough to overcome the other factors.

Your first-year grades, which placed you in the 4th decile of your school, came in third. This was noticeably below the average of 6th decile among accepted students and therefore nudged the outcome further toward failure.

Taken together, the low LSAT score and weaker early academic performance outweighed the positive signal from your family background, leading to the rejection.

What you should do next is focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation. A meaningful increase there would likely change future predictions in your favor and open doors to both admission and bar exam success.
